uni-chem-core.title: Chemical Engineering core
uni-chem-core.description: Core B.Tech chemical engineering: material and energy balances, fluid flow and heat transfer, separation processes, reaction engineering and process control, with solved numericals and process-plant labs. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.Tech programmes.

steps.title: Steady-state balance
steps.body: For a steady process with no reaction: **input = output** for total mass and for every component. Always draw a flow diagram and label every stream.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Stream A: 100 kg/h at 20 wt% NaCl. Stream B: 50 kg/h at 50 wt% NaCl.

Total out = 150 kg/h. Salt in = 0.20×100 + 0.50×50 = 20 + 25 = 45 kg/h. Salt fraction = 45/150 = 0.30.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Averaging the two percentages (35%) ignores that the streams have different flow rates. Always weight by mass flow.

scenes.text: A new plant converts only 50% of reactant A per pass, but the owner wants no loss of A.
You must size the recycle line.

steps.title: Recycle logic
steps.body: Single-pass conversion = reacted/fed to reactor. Overall conversion = reacted/fresh feed. A separator returning unreacted A makes overall conversion approach 100% even when single-pass is low.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Fresh feed F = 100 mol/h A; all unreacted A is recycled; single-pass X = 0.5. Reactor feed = F + R. A reacted must equal 100 (overall X = 1), so 0.5(F + R) = 100, giving F + R = 200 and R = 100 mol/h.

steps.title: Mistake
steps.body: Put the balance boundary around the whole process for overall quantities and around the reactor or mixing point for internal ones; mixing the boundaries gives wrong equations.

scenes.text: A boiler house burns 100 mol/h of methane with 20% excess air.
You must set the air blower and predict the flue gas nitrogen.

steps.title: Stoichiometry
steps.body: CH4 + 2 O2 → CO2 + 2 H2O. Air is 21 mol% O2 and 79 mol% N2. Excess air % = (O2 supplied − O2 theoretical)/O2 theoretical × 100.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Theoretical O2 = 2×100 = 200 mol/h. With 20% excess: 240 mol/h. Air = 240/0.21 = 1142.9 mol/h. N2 = 0.79×1142.9 = 902.9 mol/h.

steps.title: Mistake
steps.body: Excess air is on theoretical O2, not on total air consumed; for complete combustion the two coincide only if you track unconsumed O2 correctly.

lessons.title: Lab: Sensible heat duty of a water heater

scenes.text: A hostel needs 1000 kg/h of hot water at 85 °C from 25 °C.
The electrician asks for the heater rating in kW.

steps.title: Formula
steps.body: For a flowing stream with no phase change, **Q = ṁ cp ΔT**. Convert kJ/h to kW by dividing by 3600.

steps.title: Mistake
steps.body: Do not mix kJ with J or hours with seconds; ΔT in °C equals ΔT in K.

scenes.text: A food plant heats a kettle with saturated steam at 1 atm.
You must know the heat released as the steam condenses.

steps.title: Latent heat
steps.body: During condensation at constant temperature, **Q = ṁ λ**. For water at 100 °C and 1 atm, λ ≈ 2257 kJ/kg.

steps.title: Why steam
steps.body: Latent heat is large and delivered at near-constant temperature, so steam is a preferred industrial heating medium.

scenes.text: A pilot burner consumes methane at 10 mol/s.

steps.title: Standard heat of combustion
steps.body: For CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + H2O(l), ΔH°c ≈ −890 kJ/mol at 25 °C. Negative means heat is released (exothermic).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: 10 mol/s × 890 kJ/mol = 8900 kJ/s = 8900 kW.

steps.title: Mistake
steps.body: Heat released uses the liquid-water heat of combustion (higher heating value); for steam in flue gas the lower heating value (about 802 kJ/mol) applies.

lessons.title: Lab: Is the pipe flow turbulent?

scenes.text: A 50 mm line carries water at 1 m/s.

steps.title: Reynolds number
steps.body: **Re = ρvD/μ**. In pipes: laminar below ~2100, transitional 2100–4000, turbulent above ~4000.

steps.title: Mistake
steps.body: Use dynamic viscosity (Pa·s) with ρ in kg/m³; using centipoise without converting is the most common slip.

steps.title: Power
steps.body: Hydraulic power = ρ g Q H. Shaft power = hydraulic ÷ efficiency.

steps.title: Margin

steps.title: Relative volatility

steps.title: Mistake
steps.body: α = 1 means no separation is possible by distillation.

scenes.text: Operators run the column at total reflux to test its trays.
The design engineer needs the theoretical minimum stages.

steps.title: Fenske equation
steps.body: **Nmin = ln[(xD/(1−xD))·((1−xB)/xB)] / ln α**, including the reboiler as a stage.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: xD = 0.95, xB = 0.05, α = 2.5: numerator ln(19×19)=ln361=5.889; denominator ln2.5 = 0.916; Nmin = 6.43.

steps.title: Use
steps.body: Nmin is a lower bound: real columns need more stages and an actual reflux ratio.

steps.title: CSTR design
steps.body: Perfect mixing: exit equals tank concentration. First-order: **X = kτ/(1+kτ)**.

steps.title: Note
steps.body: Rate is evaluated at exit conditions, so CSTRs need more volume than PFRs for the same conversion in positive-order reactions.

Management asks which reactor is better.

steps.title: PFR
steps.body: For first-order: **X = 1 − e^(−kτ)**.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: kτ = 2: X = 1 − e⁻² = 1 − 0.1353 = 0.8647 → 86.5%, compared with 66.7% for the CSTR.

steps.title: Why
steps.body: In a PFR concentration falls gradually, so average rate stays higher than in a CSTR.

steps.title: P action
steps.body: **u = ubias + Kc·e**, with e = setpoint − measurement.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: ubias = 12 mA, Kc = 4 mA per %, e = 1.5 % gives u = 12 + 6 = 18 mA.

steps.title: Mistake
steps.body: P-only control leaves an offset; use integral action to remove it.

steps.title: ZN table
steps.body: P: Kc = 0.5Ku. PI: Kc = 0.45Ku, τI = Pu/1.2. PID: Kc = 0.6Ku, τI = Pu/2, τD = Pu/8.

steps.title: Note
steps.body: ZN gives aggressive tuning (quarter decay); detune for safety-critical loops.

steps.body: For a first-order process with P control: τcl = τ/(1 + K·Kc) and offset = 1/(1 + K·Kc) of the setpoint change.

steps.body: Higher Kc speeds response and shrinks offset, but real loops with dead time become unstable.
